pedagogy.summary: This is the iteration idea: a/b is built by counting copies of the unit fraction 1/b — 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. It reframes a fraction from a static shaded region into a COUNT of equal units, exactly parallel to how a whole number is a count of ones. The pivotal move is that the count can pass the whole: iterating 1/4 past the fourth copy (4/4 = 1) gives 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — improper fractions that are perfectly ordinary numbers with a home on the number line. This unit-fraction-as-building-block view is the seed of adding fractions with like denominators (join the counts), of multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and of mixed numbers.
bestPractices: Teach 1/b as the unit you iterate, then build a/b by repeated addition of that unit — '1/5, 2/5, 3/5' spoken as 'one fifth, two fifths, three fifths' so the count is audible.
Use the number line as the primary model: start at 0 and make equal jumps of 1/b, landing on a/b; this makes iteration a physical count and naturally continues past 1 into improper fractions.
Deliberately cross the whole: iterate 1/4 to 4/4 = 1 and keep going to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting units, not as a strange new object.

Link the count to notation: the numerator IS the number of unit-fraction copies, the denominator names the unit — so 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... (seven times), and adding like fractions just adds the counts.
Contrast unit-counting with the wrong move of adding denominators (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8): on the line, two quarter-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller point, refuting it visually.
keyRepresentations: Number line with equal 1/b jumps from 0, continuing past 1 (0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4=1, 5/4, 6/4, 7/4)
Fraction strips / identical unit tiles laid end to end (seven 1/4-tiles making 7/4)
Bar model spanning more than one whole to show 7/4 as one whole plus three more quarters (1 3/4)
Skip-counting sequence in unit-fraction language ('one-fifth, two-fifths, three-fifths...')
commonMisconceptions: Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so an improper fraction like 7/4 'isn't a real/proper number' or must be an error.
Adding denominators when joining unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 rather than 2/4.
Whole-number bias in placing improper fractions: reading 7/4 as near 7 (or treating the 7 as the dominant number) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
Losing the unit: writing 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 but unable to say the denominator stays 5 because each part is the same size 1/5.
Thinking the number line 'stops' at 1 for fractions, so not continuing the jumps past the whole.

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a COUNT of unit fractions 1/b: 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. The pivotal move is letting the count pass the whole — iterating 1/4 past 4/4 = 1 to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, landing exactly on 1 3/4 — so improper fractions appear as the ordinary continuation of counting equal units on the number line, not a strange new object. This unit-as-building-block view seeds like-denominator addition (join the counts), multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and mixed numbers.

activities.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole
feedback: If a learner expects to stop at 1: iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is one more quarter landing on a definite point; a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.

If two quarter-jumps are placed at a smaller point (2/8 thinking): on the line, two equal 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not somewhere smaller; each jump is the SAME unit, so joining counts adds numerators while the unit (denominator) stays 4.
If 7/4 is placed far right near 7: count the seven small quarter-jumps together — they reach only 1 3/4, not near 7; the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
Reinforce: at the fourth jump the point is 4/4 = 1 whole, and counting does not have to stop there.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner iterate the unit themselves and watch both count and position update makes iteration a physical, audible act and makes the crossing of the whole visible — the point where improper fractions stop being strange. A live count/value tally and growing equation make the numerator=number-of-copies link concrete. Live manipulation is proposed as a way to let the learner build the count by their own action; a pre-built illustration (below) conveys the same decomposition but without the learner's own iteration.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
Pupils should understand a fraction a/b as a sum of unit fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5) and connect this to multiplication of a unit fraction by a whole number.
learnerActions: Work on a number line marked 0 to 2 with whole-number anchors at 1 and 2.
Add one 1/4 jump at a time starting from 0, saying each landing aloud: 'one quarter, two quarters, three quarters'.
Keep a running record that shows BOTH the count (number of copies) and the value n/4, alongside a growing equation 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 ...
On the fourth jump, notice the marker lands exactly on 1 and the tally reads 4/4; then deliberately keep going — tap again to step to 5/4, past the whole, still a definite point on the line.
Continue to the seventh jump, landing exactly on 1 3/4, with the equation showing seven 1/4's and the side note 7/4 = 1/4 × 7.

Switch the unit to 1/3 and repeat while keeping the whole-number anchors 1 and 2 fixed, counting up to six jumps (6/3 = 2) on this 0–2 line. To continue to seven jumps (7/3 = 2 1/3), extend the line past 2 first. Each jump is now larger: three third-jumps reach the same point 1 that four quarter-jumps reached.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is just a count of equal units 1/b; nothing forces the count to stop at the whole, so improper fractions like 7/4 are ordinary points on the line. The denominator names the size of the unit you are counting.

activities.title: Walk through a pre-built iteration and read the decomposition
feedback: If the learner thinks the count must stop at 1: point to the flap at 4/4 and the jumps beyond it — the sequence continues to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4.
If the learner loses the unit: have them restate that every tile and every jump is 1/4, so the denominator stays 4 the whole way.
activities.rationale: A pre-built reveal communicates the decomposition and crossing-the-whole clearly and is useful when a live iterator is unavailable; its limit is that the count is pre-baked rather than built by the learner's own action, so pair it with construction when possible.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Study a 0–2 number line showing seven quarter-jumps, revealing the running total jump by jump (1/4, 2/4, ... 7/4).
At the 4/4 mark, read the flap '= 1 whole, keep going' and continue tracing to 7/4.
Read the side card showing 7/4 = 1/4 × 7 and 7/4 = 1 3/4.
Lay out seven identical quarter-tiles end to end and match them to the seven jumps, then state in words that each part is the same size 1/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Seven copies of 1/4 decompose 7/4, the count continues naturally past 1, and 7/4 equals exactly 1 3/4 — the same unit-count read from a worked layout.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where do seven quarter-jumps land?
feedback: Full understanding looks like: seven equal 1/4-jumps passing 4/4 = 1 without pause to land exactly on 1 3/4, 7/4 written as seven 1/4's, and 7/4 justified as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point — with the same reasoning transferred to 7/3 on request.
Partial understanding: iterates and writes the sum correctly but hesitates to cross the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY in terms of counting units.

If the learner says 7/4 'isn't a real fraction' or 'isn't a number', or stops at 1: iterate aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each one more quarter on a definite point. (7/4 is indeed an improper fraction, but it is still a real number.)
If the learner writes 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 or growing denominators: show two 1/4-jumps landing at 2/4 and re-establish that joining equal units adds numerators while the unit stays 4.
activities.rationale: The reason behind the prediction is the diagnostic part: a learner expecting the jumps to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. The second-tier 'how do you know it's a number' separates lucky placement from understanding. This surfaces outcomes and misconceptions rather than teaching the iteration, so it complements, not replaces, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Before making any jumps, PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land — before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and state WHY.
Iterate the seven quarter-jumps, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing exactly on 1 3/4.
Explain any mismatch between the prediction and the result.

Answer probing questions: Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7 when there's a 7 in it? If it were 7/3 instead of 7/4, would the jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0, and why? When you write 7/4 as seven 1/4's, why does the bottom number stay 4 and not grow? At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1 — what is that point as a fraction, and why doesn't counting have to stop there?
Write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions and answer: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason, not just a landing spot, reveals whether the learner holds the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief or the add-denominators error, and distinguishes a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding that 7/4 is a count of seven units.

activities.title: Spot and refute the add-denominators move
feedback: Correct: two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4 — adding denominators would wrongly shrink the result; each jump is the same 1/4.
If jumps shrink across the sum: re-establish that every term is the identical unit 1/4, so the size does not change as you add more.

In ordering 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4: 7/4 sits between 5/4 and 9/4 and lands at exactly 1 3/4 on the line, while 9/4 lands at 2 1/4 (just past 2) — compare by the count of quarters, not the numerator against unrelated wholes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting unit-counting with the common add-denominators error and refuting it visually on the line targets a specific, documented misconception directly; the number line makes the equal-size units concrete.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 and test it on the number line by making two equal quarter-jumps from 0.
Mark where the two jumps actually land and compare it with where 2/8 would sit.
State in your own words why joining two copies of the same unit gives 2/4, not 2/8.

Answer a quick check: 5/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 + __ (fill the remaining 1/8 terms to make five eighths — three more are needed); then order 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4 on a line long enough to reach 9/4 (use a 0–3 line, since 9/4 = 2 1/4 lies past 2).
activities.intendedInsight: Joining unit fractions keeps the unit (denominator) fixed and adds the counts (numerators); the jumps stay the same size.

constraints: Use the number line as the primary model with equal 1/b jumps from 0, extending past 1 so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting; this representation is recommended by the cited guide.
Speak the count aloud ('one fifth, two fifths, three fifths') so the iteration is audible and the numerator is heard as the number of copies.
Deliberately cross the whole (4/4 = 1, then 5/4, 6/4, 7/4) rather than stopping at 1.

Keep the denominator fixed while counting copies of a unit. If the denominator changes, keep the whole-number anchors fixed and change the jump size: thirds reach1 in three jumps, quarters in four jumps.
When a task uses values beyond a whole (e.g. ordering up to 9/4 = 2 1/4), draw the line long enough to contain them rather than clipping to 0–2.
A pre-built reveal or worked illustration conveys the decomposition but does not have the learner iterate themselves; pair it with learner construction when possible.
Unit tiles and fraction strips are physical approximations of the ideal equal jumps; keep each tile the same size to represent equal units.

A quiz or fill-in check can verify the outcome (expressing a/b as a sum, placing an improper fraction), but recognition or selection alone may not elicit the learner's own construction of the sum or placement; use such checks alongside tasks where the learner builds and justifies, not as the sole learning surface.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The original row rated in-role dialogue and 3D rendering as 'poor' fit; these were catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws. They are reframed as narrowly scoped observations (iterating a unit along a line is inherently 1D/planar; a narrating character adds little over learner-built iteration) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach.

Arithmetic checked: 7/4 = 1 3/4 EXACTLY (one whole plus three quarters), so seven 1/4-jumps land ON 1 3/4, not 'just past' it; seven 1/4's sum to 7/4; two 1/4's sum to 2/4; after two 1/8 terms, three further 1/8 terms are needed to total 5/8; 9/4 = 2 1/4. The ordering feedback references the set's actual neighbours (5/4 and 9/4) and now uses a 0–3 line so 9/4 fits.
The original row's probeDeeper and correctAnswer described 7/4 as a point 'just past 1 3/4'; this is an original error (7/4 = 1 3/4 exactly) and has been corrected in all learner-facing text here.
The add-denominators distractor (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, or 7/4 = 7/28) is intentionally presented only as a wrong move to refute, never as a valid answer.
Recognition/selection checks are scoped as not themselves eliciting independent construction (an observable affordance limit), not as a categorical 'quiz only assesses' claim.

assess.poeTask: Before making any jumps, ask the child to PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land: before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and to say WHY. The stated reason is the diagnostic part: a child expecting it to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. Then iterate the seven quarter-jumps together, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing at 1 3/4, and have the child explain the mismatch with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You made seven jumps and landed just past 1 3/4. Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7, when there's a 7 in it?
What if the fraction had been 7/3 instead of 7/4 — would your jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0? Why?
When you write 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... seven times, why does the bottom number stay 4 the whole way and not grow?
At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1. What is that point as a fraction, and why does the counting not have to stop there?
assess.correctAnswer: Seven equal jumps of 1/4 from 0, landing at 1 3/4; 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. Yes, 7/4 is a real number — it is seven quarters, a definite point just past 1 3/4 on the line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so 7/4 'isn't a proper number' or must be a mistake — stops the jumps at 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 on the line: 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is just one more quarter and lands on a definite point. Reteach that a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 isn't a proper number — the top can't be bigger than the bottom, so it must be written a different way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to place 7/4 beyond 1, or says it should be written only as a mixed number because '7/4 isn't allowed'; answers the second tier with 'it's not a real fraction'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds denominators when summing unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, so the sum can never build to 7/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the line, two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller 2/8 point. Re-establish that each jump is the SAME unit 1/4, so joining counts adds numerators while the denominator (the unit) stays 4.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... = 7/28, because you add the bottoms too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/4 as a sum whose terms have growing denominators, or claims 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8; the jumps get smaller instead of staying equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: places 7/4 near 7 (or treats the 7 as dominant) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarters together onto the line so 7/4 is felt as seven small jumps reaching only 1 3/4. Contrast with 7 whole-ones. Reteach that the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 is close to 7 on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Marks 7/4 far to the right near 7, or orders it as if larger than 6/4-and-under by the numerator alone without regard to the unit.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a/b by iterating 1/b; stops at 1, denies 7/4 is a number, or adds denominators so the sum never reaches 7/4. Reads the numerator as a whole-number magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Makes seven equal 1/4-jumps, passes 4/4 = 1 without pause to land at 1 3/4, writes 7/4 as the sum of seven 1/4's, and justifies 7/4 as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point on the line. Explains the denominator names the unit being counted and transfers the reasoning to a different unit (e.g. 7/3) on request.
responseLevels.partial: Iterates 1/b correctly and writes 7/4 as seven 1/4's, but hesitates at or cannot justify crossing the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY it is a legitimate number in terms of counting units — lists the copies without the relational 'count of a unit' reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show 7/4 on a number line from 0 to 2 by making equal jumps, and write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions. Then tell me: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands iteration counts seven equal 1/4-units, passes 4/4 = 1 without stopping, and defends 7/4 as an ordinary number. A child who believes fractions must be less than 1 balks at the improper form, stops at 1, or declares 7/4 'not proper'. A child who adds denominators writes 1/4+1/4=2/8 and cannot make the sum reach 7/4. The second tier — 'how do you know it's a number' — separates a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding of the unit-count.
